subject: DI02000121

intro_text.en: Unit 2 of Mechanical Drafting (DI02000121) teaches you to read and draw sectional orthographic views: why hidden interiors force us to cut the object with an imaginary cutting plane, the vocabulary of sections (cutting plane, section lines/hatching), the seven standard types of section - full, half, revolved, removed, partial, offset and aligned - and the routine for producing a sectional view from an isometric drawing or a physical object, which is the core skill of Practical 3.
intro_text.gu: Unit 2 of Mechanical Drafting (DI02000121) teaches you to read and draw sectional orthographic views: why hidden interiors force us to cut the object with an imaginary cutting plane, the vocabulary of sections (cutting plane, section lines/hatching), the seven standard types of section - full, half, revolved, removed, partial, offset and aligned - and the routine for producing a sectional view from an isometric drawing or a physical object, which is the core skill of Practical 3.

title.en: 2.1-2.2 Orthographic reading and the need for sections
title.gu: 2.1-2.2 Orthographic reading and the need for sections

body.en:
Reading = reconstructing the solid from flat views

Orthographic reading is the skill of building the true 3-D shape of an object in your mind from its 2-D front, top and side views. The views are not three separate pictures: they are one object projected onto three mutually perpendicular planes (first-angle projection is the standard practice for this course - FV placed above TV, the view from the left placed on the right). Lengths agree between FV and TV (vertical projectors), heights agree between FV and SV, and widths between TV and SV; every point, edge and surface must be traceable through all the views.

How a trained reader works

  • Identify the main view (usually FV - the most descriptive face) and locate each feature (hole, step, rib, slot) in at least two views before deciding its shape: a rectangle in FV with a circle in TV is a cylinder/hole, never a square.
  • Distinguish solid material from void: lines mean edges - a visible line is an edge you could touch from that direction, a hidden (dashed) line is an edge behind material.
  • Check consistency: every line must 'close' - an edge ending in mid-air, or a hole shown in one view and absent in the projector of another, marks a wrong reading (or a wrong drawing).

Why reading matters before drawing

Manufacturing reads drawings far more often than it makes them; a misread view becomes a scrapped part. Unit 2 therefore practises reading on sectioned objects, where the interior - invisible in plain views - is the whole problem.

h.en: 2.2 Need of sections, section lines and cutting plane
h.gu: 2.2 Need of sections, section lines and cutting plane

body.en:
The problem: interiors drown in hidden lines

A hollow or internally-featured part (housing, cylinder block, hub with keyway) drawn in plain orthographic views fills up with dashed hidden lines that cross, overlap and become unreadable - and a dimension cannot be attached clearly to a dashed line. The solution used worldwide: imagine the object cut by a plane, remove the nearer part, and draw what the cut reveals as solid visible geometry.

The three terms (use them precisely)

  • Cutting plane: the imaginary plane that slices the object, drawn on the adjacent view as a cutting-plane line (thick chain) with arrows showing the direction of viewing and capital letters (A-A, B-B...). The section view is named after it: 'SECTION A-A'.
  • Sectional view: the view of the remaining part after the nearer half is imagined removed; outlines beyond the plane are drawn visible.
  • Section lines (hatching): thin parallel lines (normally 45 deg, spaced about 2-4 mm) drawn only on the surfaces actually cut by the plane. Voids, holes and air are never hatched. Adjacent parts in an assembly get different angles/spacings (Unit 5).

Hatching rules that examiners check

  • Same part = same angle and spacing in all its sectioned views; do not hatch thin features the long way (ribs, webs, spokes, shafts, bolts and nuts are conventionally NOT section-lined when cut longitudinally - Unit 4/5 use this).
  • Hidden lines are normally omitted inside a sectional view - the section exists to replace them.
  • Very thin material (sheet, gasket) may be shown solid black instead of hatched.

title.en: 2.3-2.4 Types of sections and drawing sectional views
title.gu: 2.3-2.4 Types of sections and drawing sectional views

h.en: 2.3 Types of sections and their applications
h.gu: 2.3 Types of sections and their applications

body.en:
The seven standard types

  • Full section: the cutting plane passes straight through the whole object; one complete half is removed. Use for unsymmetrical hollow parts (housings, blocks) where the full interior matters.
  • Half section: two planes at right angles remove one quarter; one half of the view is external, the other half sectional, divided by the centre line. Use only for symmetrical objects (flanges, covers) - shows inside and outside in a single view, saving a view.
  • Revolved section: the cross-section of a bar/arm is drawn revolved 90 deg onto the view itself, at the position of the cut. Use for spokes, arms, bars and extrusions whose varying cross-section must be shown without extra views.
  • Removed section: the same cross-section, but drawn outside the view, often enlarged and labelled. Use when the view is crowded or the profile is the main information (aircraft/ship sections, channels).
  • Partial (broken-out) section: only a local region is cut away, bounded by a freehand break line. Use to expose one small internal feature (a drilled oil hole, a keyway) without sectioning the whole part.
  • Offset section: the cutting plane is stepped (offset) to pass through features that do not lie in one plane - e.g. several holes on different axes; the steps are not drawn in the sectional view. Use for plates and blocks with scattered holes.
  • Aligned section: features arranged radially (holes on a bolt circle, arms) are imagined revolved into the cutting plane and then projected, so their true spacing from the centre appears. Use for flanges and wheels.

Choosing the type (the design decision)

Ask: what must be revealed, and is the object symmetrical? Reveal everything in an unsymmetrical part - full; symmetrical part - half; only a profile - revolved/removed; only one detail - partial; features off one plane - offset; features around a circle - aligned. The fewer conventions the reader must decode, the better the drawing.

h.en: 2.4 Drawing sectional views from isometric drawings / physical objects
h.gu: 2.4 Drawing sectional views from isometric drawings / physical objects

body.en:
The standard task

Given an isometric drawing (or the physical object) and cutting-plane conditions (plane position and viewing direction), produce the sectional orthographic views - the exact skill of Practical 3 and the commonest drawing question of this unit. The diagram works one: a stepped block with a vertical hole, cut by an axial plane A-A.

Routine (follow it every time)

  • Step 1 - read the object: list the basic solids (two rectangular blocks + one cylindrical hole) and which view the cutting plane appears as an edge in (here the TV/FV pair).
  • Step 2 - mark the cutting plane on that view with the cutting-plane line, arrows pointing in the direction of sight, letters A-A. The half the arrows point away from is removed.
  • Step 3 - draw the sectional view: every edge cut or visible beyond the plane becomes a visible line; hatch only the solid material the plane passes through; the hole stays blank; omit hidden lines inside the section.
  • Step 4 - project the companion views unchanged (top view here), aligned on the same projectors, and dimension after the geometry reads correctly.

Conventions and traps

  • Ribs, webs, lugs, spokes and arms cut lengthwise are left unhatched (they would look falsely thick); cut crosswise, they are hatched.
  • Standard parts - shafts, bolts, nuts, screws, keys, pins, rivets - are never section-lined when the plane passes along their axis.
  • In a half section, hidden lines are omitted from both halves and the dividing line is the centre line, not a visible line.
  • The direction of hatching and viewing arrows must agree - a reversed arrow flips the whole section.

h.en: Practical 3: Drawing of sectional orthographic views
h.gu: Practical 3: Drawing of sectional orthographic views

body.en:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 3)

From given isometric drawings/physical objects and stated cutting-plane conditions, draw the sectional orthographic views - sketchbook first, then the A2 sheet.

Procedure

  • Step 1: Read the object; sketch the uncut FV/TV/SV lightly and verify projections agree.
  • Step 2: Mark the cutting plane (line + arrows + letters) on the view where it shows as an edge.
  • Step 3: Draw the sectional view: visible outlines, 45 deg hatching on cut material only, voids blank, ribs/shafts unsectioned per convention.
  • Step 4: Complete the remaining views, dimension the internal features from the sectional view, and label 'SECTION A-A'.

Result (report format)

Submit the sheet with at least the assigned objects sectioned as specified. In the conclusion, name the section type used for each object and why, and state one convention you applied (e.g., rib not hatched, hidden lines omitted).

h.en: Q1. Why are sectional views necessary? Explain with the help of a suitable example.
h.gu: Q1. Why are sectional views necessary? Explain with the help of a suitable example.

body.en:
Model answer

Objects with internal features - holes, cavities, counterbores - drawn in plain orthographic views are covered with hidden (dashed) lines that overlap and cannot be dimensioned clearly. A sectional view removes this confusion: the object is imagined cut by a cutting plane, the nearer portion removed, and the interior drawn as visible outlines with the cut material hatched. Example: a flanged bush with a stepped bore - plain FV shows three pairs of dashed lines for the bore steps; SECTION A-A through the axis shows the bore profile directly, so its diameters and depths can be dimensioned and manufactured. Sections therefore (i) reveal internal shape, (ii) replace hidden lines with visible ones, (iii) allow internal dimensioning, and (iv) often save an extra view.

h.en: Q2. Define: cutting plane, section lines, sectional view. Draw the cutting-plane symbol.
h.gu: Q2. Define: cutting plane, section lines, sectional view. Draw the cutting-plane symbol.

body.en:
Model answer

The cutting plane is the imaginary plane that slices the object to expose the interior; it is drawn as a thick long-short-dash (chain) line, thickened at the ends and at changes of direction, with arrowheads showing the direction of viewing and capital letters (A, B...) identifying it. Section lines (hatching) are thin lines drawn at 45 deg (uniform 2-4 mm spacing) on the surface actually cut by the plane of section. The sectional view is the view obtained after imagining the part between the viewer and the cutting plane removed; it is labelled with the plane letters, e.g. SECTION A-A. The symbol: a chain-thick line across the object with bold arrows at both ends pointing in the viewing direction and the same capital letter placed at each end.

h.en: Q3. Explain full section and half section. When is each used?
h.gu: Q3. Explain full section and half section. When is each used?

body.en:
Model answer

In a full section the cutting plane passes entirely through the object and one complete half is imagined removed; the whole view is sectional. It is used for unsymmetrical hollow parts whose complete interior must be shown. In a half section two cutting planes at right angles remove one quarter of the object; one half of the resulting view shows the exterior and the other half the sectioned interior, separated by the centre line. It is used only for symmetrical objects such as flanges and covers, because it shows internal and external features in one view and saves drawing an additional view. Hidden lines are omitted in both; in half section the divide is a centre line, never a visible edge.

h.en: Q4. Differentiate between revolved section and removed section.
h.gu: Q4. Differentiate between revolved section and removed section.

body.en:
Model answer

Both show the true cross-section of a bar, arm or spoke at a marked position. A revolved section is drawn revolved 90 deg directly on top of the view at the cutting position; the object outline is broken around it. A removed section is taken out and drawn elsewhere on the sheet, frequently to an enlarged scale, and identified by the cutting-plane letters (e.g. SECTION B-B). Revolved sections suit small profiles where the view has spare room; removed sections suit important or large profiles, crowded views, and cases where several sections of one long part must be compared.

h.en: Q5. What is an offset section? Why are the offsets not shown in the sectional view?
h.gu: Q5. What is an offset section? Why are the offsets not shown in the sectional view?

body.en:
Model answer

An offset section uses a cutting plane that is stepped - offset in parallel segments - so that one sectional view can pass through several features that do not lie in a single straight plane, such as holes drilled on different axes of a plate. The bends (offsets) of the plane are marked on the plan view by the cutting-plane line, but they are not drawn as lines in the sectional view itself, because the bends are imaginary - no edge of the object exists there; drawing them would invent false edges and confuse the reader. The section is labelled with the end letters only (SECTION A-A).

h.en: Q6. State any four hatching (section-lining) rules.
h.gu: Q6. State any four hatching (section-lining) rules.

body.en:
Model answer

(1) Hatch only the material actually cut by the plane; holes and voids are left blank. (2) Section lines are thin, normally at 45 deg to the main outline, evenly spaced about 2-4 mm. (3) The same part keeps the same hatch angle and spacing in every sectioned view; adjacent parts in an assembly differ in angle or spacing. (4) Ribs, webs, spokes and standard parts (shafts, bolts, nuts) cut longitudinally are conventionally not hatched; hidden lines are normally omitted in sectional views. (Any four correct rules.)

h.en: Q7. What is a partial (broken-out) section? Where is it applied?
h.gu: Q7. What is a partial (broken-out) section? Where is it applied?

body.en:
Model answer

A partial section cuts away only a small local portion of the object to reveal one internal detail, the cut region being bounded by a thin freehand break line instead of a full cutting plane, and the exposed cut surface being hatched. It is applied when only one small feature needs explanation - an oil hole in a shaft, a keyway in a hub, a local thread relief - and a full or half section would waste effort and destroy useful external detail. No cutting-plane line is drawn; the break line itself shows the extent of the cut.

h.en: Q8. What is an aligned section? Give one application.
h.gu: Q8. What is an aligned section? Give one application.

body.en:
Model answer

An aligned section is used for objects with features arranged around an axis - holes on a bolt circle, spokes, arms. The cutting plane is bent through the axis and the feature, and the feature is imagined revolved (aligned) into that plane before being projected, so the sectional view shows its true radial distance and size. Application: a flange with six equispaced bolt holes - the aligned section shows two opposite holes at their correct pitch-circle radius, instead of the foreshortened positions a straight plane would miss entirely.

q.gu: Why do we draw sectional views?

q.en: What does the arrow on a cutting-plane line mean?
q.gu: What does the arrow on a cutting-plane line mean?

a.en: The direction of viewing the sectional view; the part on the side the arrows point away from is imagined removed.
a.gu: The direction of viewing the sectional view; the part on the side the arrows point away from is imagined removed.

q.en: Which surfaces get hatched?
q.gu: Which surfaces get hatched?

a.en: Only the solid material actually cut by the cutting plane. Holes, cavities and air spaces are left blank.
a.gu: Only the solid material actually cut by the cutting plane. Holes, cavities and air spaces are left blank.

q.en: Angle and spacing of section lines?
q.gu: Angle and spacing of section lines?

a.en: Thin lines, usually at 45 degrees, evenly spaced about 2 to 4 mm; angle changed to 30/60 degrees if 45 would run parallel to a main outline.
a.gu: Thin lines, usually at 45 degrees, evenly spaced about 2 to 4 mm; angle changed to 30/60 degrees if 45 would run parallel to a main outline.

q.en: Half section can be used for which objects?
q.gu: Half section can be used for which objects?

a.en: Only symmetrical objects - one quarter is removed so one half-view is external, the other sectional, divided by the centre line.
a.gu: Only symmetrical objects - one quarter is removed so one half-view is external, the other sectional, divided by the centre line.

q.en: Rib cut lengthwise - hatched or not?
q.gu: Rib cut lengthwise - hatched or not?

a.en: Not hatched, by convention; hatching it would make the rib look like thick solid material across the whole view.
a.gu: Not hatched, by convention; hatching it would make the rib look like thick solid material across the whole view.

q.en: Are bolts and shafts section-lined in assembly sections?
q.gu: Are bolts and shafts section-lined in assembly sections?

a.en: No. Standard parts and shafts cut by a plane along their axis are conventionally shown unsectioned.
a.gu: No. Standard parts and shafts cut by a plane along their axis are conventionally shown unsectioned.

q.en: Difference between revolved and removed section?
q.gu: Difference between revolved and removed section?

a.en: Revolved: cross-section drawn revolved onto the view itself. Removed: drawn outside the view, labelled (SECTION B-B), possibly enlarged.
a.gu: Revolved: cross-section drawn revolved onto the view itself. Removed: drawn outside the view, labelled (SECTION B-B), possibly enlarged.

q.en: What is an offset section?
q.gu: What is an offset section?

a.en: A section whose cutting plane is stepped to pass through features lying in different planes; the steps appear on the cutting-plane line but not as lines in the sectional view.
a.gu: A section whose cutting plane is stepped to pass through features lying in different planes; the steps appear on the cutting-plane line but not as lines in the sectional view.

q.en: Why are hidden lines omitted in a sectional view?

title.en: Practical 3: Drawing of sectional orthographic views
title.gu: Practical 3: Drawing of sectional orthographic views

body.en:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 3)

From given isometric drawings/physical objects and stated cutting-plane conditions, draw the sectional orthographic views - sketchbook first, then the A2 sheet.

Procedure

  • Step 1: Read the object; sketch the uncut FV/TV/SV lightly and verify projections agree.
  • Step 2: Mark the cutting plane (line + arrows + letters) on the view where it shows as an edge.
  • Step 3: Draw the sectional view: visible outlines, 45 deg hatching on cut material only, voids blank, ribs/shafts unsectioned per convention.
  • Step 4: Complete the remaining views, dimension the internal features from the sectional view, and label 'SECTION A-A'.

Result (report format)

Submit the sheet with at least the assigned objects sectioned as specified. In the conclusion, name the section type used for each object and why, and state one convention you applied (e.g., rib not hatched, hidden lines omitted).
